drapeaux.note: The Gospel verse is rendered from the French, which itself translates the English version Merton cites; Merton's exact English wording was not retrieved.

accroche: One man has the idea, three others carry it out and win the Nobel: the first is a footnote. Merton gave a name to this sorting.
contenu_vulgarise:
Among the Nobel laureates interviewed by the sociologist Harriet Zuckerman, one tells of a case. Two men have the same idea, and one becomes better known for it. The first goes around the laboratories looking for someone to try the experiment, no one agrees, and the idea is almost forgotten. Later, three other researchers carry it out, become famous, and win the prize. If someone had agreed back then, the laureate says, they would probably have published together and the first man would be known. As it is, he is a footnote.

## The Mechanism

In 1968, in the journal *Science*, Robert K. Merton draws on these interviews, as well as on newspapers, letters, notebooks, scientific papers, and biographies of researchers, to describe a sorting of credit. The laureates observe that eminent researchers receive disproportionate credit for their contributions, and little-known researchers disproportionately little credit for comparable contributions. Merton locates this pattern chiefly in two cases: work co-signed by researchers of very unequal reputation, and discoveries made independently by a renowned researcher and an unknown one, where the former ordinarily receives the principal recognition. Merton names it after a verse of the Gospel according to Matthew: “For to him who has, it will be given, and he will have abundance; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (rendered from the English version Merton cites).

A physics laureate describes both sides of the phenomenon. When you are not recognized, he says, it is a little irritating to see someone find the obvious thing you had also found, and everybody credits him because he is a famous physicist. Having become famous himself, he admits that he is probably credited with ideas that others had before him. Merton sees in this a kind of rough justice, born of two injustices that offset each other: his early work was underestimated, his later work overestimated.

The effect does not stop at credit. Merton also describes an institutional version: centers of recognized excellence receive far greater resources, and their prestige attracts a disproportionate share of the most promising students. The gap is marked at the extremes. Six universities (Harvard, Berkeley, Columbia, Princeton, Caltech, and Chicago), which awarded 22% of the doctorates in the physical and biological sciences, had trained 69% of the doctorate holders who later became Nobel laureates. The top twelve universities kept 70% of the future laureates they had trained, against 28% of the other doctorate holders.

## What It Shifts

The Matthew effect is often summed up as “the rich get richer.” In Merton, the object is first of all more precise: the distribution of scientific credit. He sees in it an injustice toward the unknown, and draws from it a consequence for the circulation of ideas: the effect can increase the visibility of the contributions of recognized researchers and reduce that of the contributions of lesser-known ones.

In 1968, the argument rests on testimony, with a few figures on universities. In 2018, researchers measured the effect by comparing candidates close to a threshold: in a 2 billion euro funding program for young doctorate holders, they compared candidates just above and just below the funding cutoff. Those who cleared the cutoff accumulated more than twice as much funding over the following eight years. Part of the gap came from those who, once rejected, later applied less often elsewhere.

repere.texte: According to Merton (1968), six universities that awarded 22% of the doctorates in the physical and biological sciences had trained 69% of the doctorate holders who became Nobel laureates.
repere.source: Merton, The Matthew Effect in Science, Science, 159(3810), 1968

carte.punch: He had the idea, others got the Nobel: he is a footnote.
carte.idee: In 1968, Merton describes a sorting of credit in science: the same contribution is better recognized when it comes from an already famous researcher. In 2018, a funding study compared candidates just above and just below the cutoff: more than double over eight years.

quiz.question: What does Merton describe in 1968 under the name of the Matthew effect?
choix: The tendency to credit the same contribution more when it comes from an already famous researcher
The advantage that personal wealth gives for funding one's own research
The fact that great discoveries are always the work of a single researcher
The habit of naming theories after religious texts
quiz.explication: Merton describes a distribution of scientific credit, not personal wealth: the same contribution is better recognized coming from an established name. He does not say that discoveries are solitary (he describes multiple discoveries instead), and the name comes from the verse, not from a naming habit.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the two cases Merton mainly points to, in which situation does the Matthew effect show up most clearly?
choix: When a single person works alone on a project and never publishes it
Work by researchers of unequal reputations, or independent discoveries by a renowned researcher and an unknown one
Only in fields that lack public funding
When two equally famous researchers publish the same result together
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Merton locates the effect chiefly in two cases: work co-signed by researchers of very unequal reputation, and independent discoveries by a renowned researcher and an unknown one, where the former ordinarily receives the principal recognition.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What figure does Merton give, in 1968, for the share of future Nobel laureates kept by the top twelve universities, compared with other doctorate holders?
choix: The top twelve universities kept 50% of the future laureates, on a par with the other universities
The top twelve universities trained no future Nobel laureates
The top twelve universities kept 70% of the future laureates they had trained, against 28% of the other doctorate holders
The top twelve universities trained 90% of all science doctorate holders, laureates or not
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Merton cites this figure to show the institutional Matthew effect: already prestigious centers keep a disproportionate share of their most promising students who later became laureates, against 28% for the other doctorate holders.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the 2018 study by Bol, de Vaan, and van de Rijt show about a funding program for young doctorate holders?
choix: That the amount of initial funding had no effect on the rest of the candidates' careers
That candidates just below the cutoff ended up obtaining more funding than the others
That the funding program was abolished after results judged inequitable
That candidates just above the funding cutoff accumulated more than twice as much funding over the following eight years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bol, de Vaan, and van de Rijt compare candidates just above and just below the funding cutoff: the former accumulate more than twice as much funding over eight years, a gap due in part to those who, once rejected, later apply less often elsewhere.
